strengths: High computational throughput and scalability: Built natively in JAX with end-to-end GPU vectorization, TABX achieves tens of millions of steps per second and avoids costly JIT recompilation when varying environment parameters, significantly outperforming existing frameworks like SMAX during multi-scenario training.

Rich configurability and tooling: TABX supports fine-grained reconfiguration of unit stats, continuous physics, functional terrain zones (lava, swamp, concealment bushes), and parameterized heuristic opponent policies. The inclusion of an interactive GUI scenario editor substantially lowers the barrier to creating custom benchmarks.

Principled and diverse empirical investigations: Rather than just presenting leaderboard numbers, the paper leverages the simulator's unique features to address key research questions: (1) isolating when centralized value estimation benefits from global information vs. when it degrades, (2) benchmarking intrinsic exploration (RND) in sparse-reward setups, and (3) studying multi-agent generalization via Unsupervised Environment Design (UED).

Thorough documentation and reporting: The appendix provides comprehensive implementation details, complete hyperparameter tables, wall-clock timing comparisons, and diverse evaluation metrics (win rate, episode length, first-kill rate, value error).
weaknesses: Cooperative vs. heuristic focus: Despite being pitched as a multi-agent battle simulator, the experiments focus exclusively on a cooperative team playing against parameterized heuristic bots, rather than multi-agent self-play or fully decentralized competitive/mixed-motive multi-agent learning.

Limited effectiveness of advanced UED algorithms: In the zero-shot generalization experiments (Figures 8, 29–32), sophisticated regret-based curriculum methods (PLR, ACCEL, SFL) do not noticeably outperform standard Domain Randomization (DR), particularly on unit-specification shifts. The paper would benefit from deeper diagnostic analysis into why regret-guided curricula struggle in this multi-agent setting.

Action and physics design constraints: While the environment features continuous-time physics integration and directional hurtboxes, agent movement is restricted to world-frame cardinal discrete actions rather than full continuous velocity/heading control, which slightly constrains the fidelity of physical combat dynamics.

strengths: High computational throughput and seamless reconfigurability: Implementing the simulator natively in JAX enables massive GPU parallelization. Crucially, TABX allows dynamic reconfiguration of environment parameters (unit attributes, terrain zones, physical constants) without triggering expensive JIT re-compilation, yielding orders-of-magnitude throughput gains over existing frameworks like SMAX during multi-task and curriculum training.

Comprehensive environmental design and toolchain: The inclusion of continuous 2D kinematic dynamics, directional fan-shaped fields of view, non-targeted hurtbox combat, functional terrain zones (lava, swamp, bush), and an interactive GUI scenario authoring tool provides a user-friendly and feature-rich sandbox for MARL research.

Methodological breadth across core research topics: Rather than merely providing standard benchmark scores, the paper systematically validates the environment's utility across distinct research challenges, including information-theoretic value estimation (centralized vs. independent critics), long-horizon sparse-reward exploration (RND vs. entropy), and zero-shot generalization via Unsupervised Environment Design (UED).

Thorough reporting of experimental details and complementary metrics: The appendix provides extensive documentation of unit specifications, zone properties, hyperparameter sweeps, wall-clock training times, and multiple evaluation metrics (win rate, episode length, return, and first-kill rate).
weaknesses: Conceptual similarity to existing battle environments: The core domain (top-down multi-unit skirmish / battle simulation) is already heavily explored in MARL through SMAC, SMACv2, and SMAX (JaxMARL). While the continuous hurtbox physics, terrain zones, and FoV mechanics are welcome additions, the high-level setting remains familiar.

Limited algorithmic novelty and confirmatory empirical findings: Because the work is focused on environment design, the empirical results primarily reaffirm established intuitions (e.g., centralized critics excel when occluded global state is critical; intrinsic exploration aids sparse rewards; policies struggle to generalize out-of-distribution to unit attribute shifts) without proposing new algorithmic solutions to address these shortcomings.

Reliance on rule-based heuristic adversaries: Adversaries in the benchmark tasks are driven by parameterized heuristic state machines rather than learned competitive policies or self-play, which may limit the complexity and strategic depth of adversarial counter-strategies compared to full multi-agent competitive co-evolution.

Missing code repository links: The code availability links in the Abstract and Appendix A are currently left blank; while understandable under double-blind reviewing guidelines, an open-source release with full documentation is vital to realizing the community value of an environment and benchmark paper.

strengths: High-throughput, fully vectorized JAX architecture: TABX provides efficient GPU-accelerated parallel simulation, crucially supporting dynamic parameter reconfiguration across episodes without requiring JIT recompilation.

Flexible modularity and scenario authoring: The framework introduces continuous physical interactions, directional fan-shaped fields of view, heterogeneous unit classes, and diverse terrain zones (e.g., asymmetric bush concealment, swamp drag, lava hazards), complemented by an intuitive GUI scenario editor.

Targeted empirical case studies: Rather than merely introducing a simulator, the paper demonstrates its utility through controlled studies examining when centralized critics provide value estimation advantages over independent learning, exploration challenges with RND under sparse rewards, and zero-shot generalization via Unsupervised Environment Design (UED).

Thorough benchmarking and transparency: The paper includes extensive experimental details, complete hyperparameter specifications, wall-clock time comparisons, and multiple evaluation metrics (win rate, episode length, first-kill rate, and value estimation error).
weaknesses: Adversaries rely exclusively on scripted rule-based heuristics: Opponents are governed by parameterized heuristic policies rather than learned policies or self-play competitive baselines. In multi-agent battle environments, static rule-based opponents risk overfitting and predictable behavioral exploitation.

Specific throughput evaluation framing: The benchmark comparison against SMAX in Figure 10 explicitly includes JIT recompilation overhead over 100 randomly generated scenario resets. While this demonstrates TABX's suitability for UED, standard throughput comparisons on static scenarios without recompilation overhead should also be clearly reported.

Minor presentation artifacts and typos: In Figure 10's legend, TABX is mislabeled as 'TABS'. In Section A.2, the sentence describing movement action coordinate frames is duplicated verbatim ('Movement actions are defined in a global (world) coordinate frame... Notably, the movement actions are defined within a global coordinate frame...').

strengths: High-throughput, fully GPU-accelerated implementation in JAX that avoids JIT re-compilation overhead during scenario reconfiguration, addressing a major latency bottleneck present in existing environments like SMAX.

Extensive configurability and tooling: provides parameterized unit archetypes, varied terrain zones (with asymmetric visibility and mobility penalties), customizable heuristic opponents, and an intuitive GUI scenario editor for rapid authoring.

Principled empirical studies leveraging the simulator's modularity, systematically demonstrating when centralized value learning provides structural advantages vs. when it degrades, how sparse rewards impact exploration, and highlighting that unit attribute generalization poses a significantly harder curriculum challenge than spatial layout variation in multi-agent UED.

Comprehensive benchmark evaluation and documentation, including baseline implementations for MARL (MAPPO, IPPO, QMIX, IQL) and UED (DR, PLR, PLR-perp, ACCEL, SFL), detailed timing benchmarks, and policy-vs-policy competitive payoff analyses.
weaknesses: The environment focuses exclusively on stylized combat dynamics, meaning it does not address other fundamental multi-agent challenges such as continuous resource collection, open-ended communication emergence, or complex manipulation.

While the experimental findings are solid and validate the environment's diagnostic utility, the core scientific conclusions (e.g., value estimation error under partial observability, difficulty of UED in high-dimensional agent parameter spaces) largely confirm established phenomena rather than presenting novel algorithmic frameworks.

The code repository placeholder is left blank in the manuscript ('Our code is available at:'), omitting an anonymous repository link to verify reproducibility of the simulator codebase and GUI during review.

strengths: High engineering quality and practical utility: TABX provides an end-to-end vectorized, JAX-accelerated multi-agent simulator capable of massive parallelization (>10^7 steps/sec) and dynamic parameter reconfiguration without triggering expensive JIT recompilation overhead, which is a major bottleneck in existing frameworks like SMAX.

Rich and realistic interaction mechanics: Unlike standard gridworlds or point-mass battle simulators with target-locking, TABX introduces continuous-like physics with directional movement, fan-shaped fields of view, hurtbox-based non-targeted hit detection, and tactical terrain zones (concealing bushes, damage-inducing lava, movement-attenuating swamps).

Principled and thorough experimental investigations: Rather than merely presenting standard win-rate curves, the paper designs controlled experiments to test fundamental MARL questions, such as the utility of centralized critics under varying degrees of viewpoint overlap (with direct value estimation error measurements), sparse-reward exploration using RND, and policy-vs-policy competitive matchups.

First-rate testbed for Multi-Agent Unsupervised Environment Design (UED): The zero-shot generalization experiments cleanly decouple unit-level attribute shifts from spatial/zone layout shifts, revealing that existing UED methods (PLR, ACCEL, SFL) struggle much more severely with high-dimensional agent-parameter curricula than topological variations.

Exceptional reproducibility and tooling: Includes a dedicated graphical scenario editor (GUI), comprehensive scenario descriptions, explicit hyperparameter tables, wall-clock timing comparisons, and diverse evaluation metrics (first-kill rates, return curves, episode lengths).
weaknesses: Domain scope restricted to battle arenas: As the authors honestly note in the limitations, TABX focuses strictly on combat dynamics (similar to SMAC and SMAX), leaving out other important MARL paradigms such as continuous communication emergence, common-pool resource management, or complex manipulation.

Coupling of low-level motor control and high-level strategy: Because units must explicitly rotate, maintain alignment, and space their attacks via hurtbox geometry, a significant portion of the sample complexity is spent learning low-level orienting and targeting rather than team coordination alone.
Incomplete placeholder in manuscript: The repository link under the Abstract ('Our code is available at:') and Section A is left blank, which should be corrected in the final camera-ready version.

strengths: High-throughput, end-to-end vectorized JAX implementation that enables massively parallel execution on GPUs and avoids expensive JIT recompilation when varying environment parameters, which is particularly beneficial for curriculum learning and Unsupervised Environment Design (UED).

Thoughtful tactical mechanics compared to existing battle benchmarks: features like fan-shaped partial observability, continuous heading and orientation requirements, directional non-targeted hurtbox interactions, and asymmetric line-of-sight concealment (bushes) create distinct, strategically richer dynamics than standard target-locking simulators.

Comprehensive empirical investigation beyond standard benchmark reporting: the paper systematically evaluates when centralized value estimation helps versus hurts (correlating empirical value error |V - V*| with return), the effects of intrinsic exploration bonuses (RND), and reveals that unit-attribute generalization is substantially harder for UED algorithms than spatial/terrain generalization.

Strong usability and accessibility features, including an interactive graphical scenario authoring tool (GUI editor), diverse baseline implementations (IPPO, MAPPO, IQL, QMIX, DR, PLR, ACCEL, SFL), and direct policy-vs-policy competitive evaluation support.
weaknesses: Domain scope is limited to stylized unit combat: while tactical mechanics differ from SMAX and SMACv2, battle simulators are already well-represented in the MARL literature, and the platform does not cover other key cooperative MARL paradigms such as continuous control, communication emergence, or economic/resource-management tasks.

Algorithmic contributions are primarily evaluative: as acknowledged in the limitations, the experiments validate the benchmark and illustrate known or intuitive phenomena rather than proposing fundamentally new MARL or UED algorithms.

The exploration study in Section 5.4 is relatively narrow, evaluating only basic entropy variations against RND within MAPPO on two hand-crafted tasks; incorporating more contemporary MARL exploration techniques would strengthen the exploration analysis.
Minor presentation omissions: repository links are left blank in the abstract and Section A (common in double-blind review, but an anonymous link or codebase confirmation is expected).
